render.title: DNA polymerase gamma copies mitochondrial DNA during division
render.body:
The enzyme responsible for copying mitochondrial DNA is DNA polymerase gamma, usually written as Pol gamma or POLG (encoded by the POLG gene). It is the only DNA polymerase that operates inside mitochondria; the nuclear DNA polymerases cannot enter the organelle.

Mitochondrial DNA replication works differently from nuclear DNA replication. Rather than opening a replication bubble and copying both strands simultaneously, mitochondria use a strand-displacement mechanism:

1. Pol gamma begins synthesising a new heavy strand starting from a specific origin of replication on the circular mitochondrial DNA.
2. As it extends the new strand, it displaces the original heavy strand, leaving it single-stranded.
3. Once the new heavy strand has been extended far enough to expose the light-strand origin, a second Pol gamma molecule begins copying the light strand in the opposite direction.
4. Both new circular DNA molecules are eventually completed and can be distributed to the two daughter mitochondria.

Pol gamma works together with accessory proteins: a processivity clamp (the Pol gamma B subunit) helps the enzyme stay attached to the DNA template for long stretches without falling off, and a helicase called TWINKLE unwinds the double-stranded DNA ahead of the polymerase.

Mutations in POLG are a known cause of mitochondrial diseases in humans, highlighting how critical this enzyme is for maintaining the mitochondrial genome across cell generations.
render.summary: Mitochondrial DNA is copied by DNA polymerase gamma (POLG). It uses a strand-displacement mechanism on the circular mitochondrial genome, assisted by the TWINKLE helicase and a processivity subunit. Mutations in POLG cause mitochondrial diseases.
